messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 18
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 55

When he is seven, the apartment down the hall shakes. It is not the wind or the old building settling. It is the sound of furniture striking plaster, of a voice splitting into something raw and unrecognizable, of heavy footsteps pacing like a trapped animal. He presses his ear against the thin wall, eyes wide, stomach knotting into a hard stone. He does not call for help. He has learned that calling for help only makes the silence afterward heavier. He sits on his bedroom floor, counting the floorboards until the footsteps stop, until the door opens and the muffled apologies begin. He repeats this pattern through primary school, then secondary, until the noise becomes less frequent but no less present in his nervous system. He grows up in a sprawling coastal suburb, carrying the quiet weight of his Oceania heritage, where stoicism is often worn like armor and family storms are kept behind closed doors. Now, at eighteen, the past does not fade. It rearranges itself into his daily habits. When he walks into a meeting room, his eyes sweep the exits before he greets anyone. When a colleague raises their voice even in jest, his pulse jumps, his breath catches, and he instinctively smooths the desk surface as if to flatten the tension. He works as a project manager for a regional logistics firm, a role he took barely a year out of high school. He is drawn to the predictable rhythm of Gantt charts and milestone reviews. He manages a team of twelve, mapping dependencies and mitigating risks with meticulous care. He knows exactly how many hours each task requires, what happens if a deadline slips, how to reroute resources before a bottleneck forms. Control is not a preference; it is a survival architecture. He tells me that if everything is documented, nothing can ambush him. His relationship with Elara began two years ago, at a coastal community festival. He remembers the salt air, the drumming, the way her laugh does not make him flinch. For the first time, closeness does not feel like a precursor to chaos. But he still wakes at 2 a.m., heart hammering, convinced he hears the familiar cadence of heavy boots on timber. He lies beside her, listening to her steady breathing, terrified that sleep will pull him back into that apartment. When stress mounts at work, he withdraws, answering texts hours later, speaking in clipped, efficient sentences. He does not want to burden her, he says, but also, he cannot risk the messiness of it spilling over. He monitors their conversations for any shift in tone, rehearsing calm responses in advance, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. He watches the rain streak the window in his apartment, the same way he used to watch the front door down the hall. His hands tremble slightly when a phone rings after ten, when a client changes a specification without warning, when a teammate misses a deadline. He adapts quickly, recalibrates, pushes through. But beneath the spreadsheets and the synchronized workflows, there is a constant, low-frequency hum of preparation for a storm that already broke. He does not know how to stop building walls, only how to keep the blueprints ready.
